description: I'm a Software Developer and Data Analytics professional from Austria, specializing in Machine Learning, Python, R, and interactive data visualization. I'm also the founder of NEURON (@neuron.machinelearning / Instagram), an educational platform focused on AI and Data Science. I'm passionate about astrophysics, space exploration, and applying ML to scientific challenges. I aim to build an innovative, data-driven solution using NASA's open datasets.
summary:
NEURON Lunar Navigator helps planners decide where and when to land near the lunar south pole. Light there is scarce: the Sun skims the horizon at about 1.6 degrees and terrain casts shadows for days. Our R/Shiny app checks, for every site and every hour, whether the Sun and the Earth are above the real local skyline, giving power and direct communication, and how long the best window lasts. It ranks sites with a transparent score and tests how stable that ranking is.

Sun and Earth positions come from JPL DE421, the skyline from NASA's LOLA 80 m elevation model, traced up to 150 km. For any clicked point, a small neural network predicts the skyline in milliseconds with 0.94 degrees error, cutting the sunlight error from 27.4 to 3.18 percentage points. We chose it over tree models because it is 68 KB, 22 times faster and smooth.

For 14 Nov to 13 Dec 2026, Mons Mouton ranks first: Sun and Earth are both up 52.8 percent of the time, with a 374 hour window from 15 Nov. It ranks first in 82.6 percent of 40,000 scenarios. Terrain matters: Nobile Rim 2 drops from 43.5 to 5.2 percent once the real skyline is used. Seven checks support this; our sunlight matches NASA illumination maps with r = 0.997.

Every number comes from scripts on NASA data. We used AI (Claude by Anthropic) to optimise code and models and to help write documents.

Find the light before you land.
details:
NEURON Lunar Navigator is an interactive web application that lets mission planners, educators and the public compare lunar south pole landing sites and dates. For each site it computes, hour by hour, whether the Sun and the Earth stand above the real local skyline. This tells the user when a lander has power and when it can talk directly to Earth. It then finds the longest continuous window where both are available.

Sun and Earth directions are computed from the JPL DE421 ephemeris in the Moon’s mean Earth frame at hourly steps. Local skylines are computed by ray marching across NASA’s LOLA 80 m digital elevation model up to 150 km, including the curvature of the Moon. Exact skylines are precomputed for all named sites and past landings. For any other point, a compact neural network (3,121 parameters, 68 KB) predicts the skyline in a few milliseconds. It was trained on 20,000 points and validated with spatial block cross-validation. Its mean error is 0.94 degrees, versus 1.47 degrees for a coarse terrain baseline and 5.53 degrees without terrain.

Sites are ranked with a transparent score that combines sunlight, Earth visibility, the longest window, communication blackouts and slope. A robustness analysis over 40,000 randomised weightings shows how stable the ranking is. For 14 November to 13 December 2026, Mons Mouton ranks first in 82.6 percent of scenarios. Both Sun and Earth are up 52.8 percent of the time there, and the best window is 374 hours long.

The interface offers a 3D map of the south pole, a timeline of light and communication windows, a side-by-side comparison, a downloadable site dossier and a “How sure are we” page with seven independent validation checks. One example: our computed sunlight agrees with NASA’s published illumination maps at 1,500 points with r = 0.997.

Tools: R and Shiny for the app, three.js for 3D, Python with NumPy, SciPy and scikit-learn for preprocessing and machine learning, and LaTeX for the technical paper.
dataRefs: JPL DE421 planetary ephemeris, used for Sun and Earth positions
NAIF lunar frame kernel (moon_080317.tf), used for the Moon’s reference frame
LOLA south pole digital elevation model at 80 m (NASA PGDA), used for real horizons and slopes
LOLA average Sun and Earth visibility maps (Mazarico et al. 2011, NASA PGDA), used for validation and machine-learning training
NASA Artemis III candidate landing regions
NASA Technical Reports Server, Artemis III regions and site locations
NSSDCA Lunar Artifact Impacts, used for coordinates of past landings
NASA Scientific Visualization Studio 8k lunar mosaic, used as the map background only
LROC (NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera), used for a landing site image
projectRefs: USGS, McClernan et al. 2024, Artemis region outlines
IAU 2015 report on cartographic coordinates and rotational elements, used for the lunar rotation model
